units.title: Unit 09 — Communicating
learningObjectives: Select idiomatic partners of say, speak, talk and tell across conversational and formal contexts.
Distinguish neutral, informal and formal reporting expressions and recognise their typical complements.
Communicate news, reasons, goals and confidential information using register-appropriate collocations.
Apply related reporting nouns and distinguish protestations of innocence from the ordinary sense of protest.

items.pt: não recusaria; aceitaria de bom grado
items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: I would not say no to an extra day of holiday.
items.note: An informal way to express a wish or willingness to accept an offer.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Needless to say, the entire team welcomed the good news.
items.note: A discourse marker introducing something the speaker considers obvious.

items.pt: é óbvio; nem precisa ser dito
items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: It goes without saying that confidential files must remain secure.
items.note: Introduces an expectation presented as too obvious to need explanation.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: During the presentation, Daniel did not say a word.
items.note: Say takes the word spoken as object; tell is not normally used in this phrase.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Generally speaking, customers prefer short and clear instructions.
items.note: Used to qualify a broad generalisation rather than a strict universal claim.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Strictly speaking, the document is a draft rather than a contract.
items.note: Introduces a precise or technical distinction that qualifies what was said.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Former students still speak highly of their chemistry teacher.
items.note: Speak highly of someone means express praise or a favourable opinion.

items.pt: falar de maneira clara ou adequada
items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: The actor practised speaking properly before recording the announcement.
items.note: Typically concerns clear or acceptable speech; can sound patronising when directed at adults.

items.pt: falar de negócios; tratar de assuntos profissionais
items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: After the introductions, the partners sat down to talk business.
items.note: Means discuss professional or commercial matters rather than socialise.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Ignore that rumour; the anonymous commentator is talking nonsense.
items.note: Nonsense is the usual noun with talk when speech has no sensible content.

items.pt: falar com sensatez; dizer coisas sensatas
items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Once everyone had calmed down, Priya began to talk sense.
items.note: The positive counterpart to talk nonsense; usually used without an article.

items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: Marta would only tell a secret to someone she trusted.
items.note: Tell naturally takes a person or the information conveyed as its complement.

items.pt: ler a sorte de alguém; prever o futuro de alguém
items.section: A · Say, speak, talk and tell
items.example: At the fair, a performer offered to tell visitors' fortunes.
items.note: A conventional phrase for supposedly predicting a person’s future.

items.pt: dar uma razão; apresentar um motivo
items.example: The manager refused to give a reason for the sudden cancellation.
items.note: Give a reason is idiomatic; say a reason is not the normal choice.

items.example: Applicants should give reasons for requesting an extension.
items.note: Reasons commonly follows give when justifying a choice or position.

items.example: The research proposal must state an aim that can be measured.
items.note: State is formal and precise, especially with aim, purpose or goal.

items.example: The presenter stated a purpose for the workshop before inviting questions.
items.note: State your purpose is more formal than simply say what you want.

items.example: The introduction should state a goal for the next quarter.
items.note: State a goal is a conventional formal reporting combination.

items.example: Visitors must state their business at the security desk.
items.note: Formal or institutional phrase meaning explain why you are present.

items.example: The witness agreed to give an account of the incident.
items.note: Account here means an oral or written description of what happened.

items.example: The engineer gave a detailed account of the equipment failure.
items.note: Detailed modifies account to emphasise thoroughness in a report.

items.example: The diagrams helped the instructor get the message across.
items.note: Informal combination meaning successfully communicate the intended idea.

items.example: The judges declared the youngest competitor the winner.
items.note: Declare formally announces a status or decision.

items.pt: declarar oficialmente o óbito de alguém
items.example: After examining the patient, the doctor pronounced him dead.
items.note: A formal medical and legal pronouncement, not an ordinary synonym of say.

items.example: Experienced volunteers impart knowledge through practical workshops.
items.note: Impart is a relatively formal verb meaning pass on knowledge or information.

items.example: Her grandmother tried to impart wisdom without giving orders.
items.note: Wisdom commonly pairs with impart to describe passing on insight.

items.example: The briefing aimed to impart facts rather than speculation.
items.note: Formal wording for making factual information known.

items.example: He promised he would not divulge a secret entrusted to him.
items.note: Divulge suggests disclosing something that was intended to remain private.

items.example: The journalist refused to divulge sources during the hearing.
items.note: Used for revealing confidential information about where reports originated.

items.example: Staff must not divulge confidential details of ongoing negotiations.
items.note: A formal disclosure verb particularly appropriate to sensitive information.

items.example: The health agency used local radio to disseminate information.
items.note: Disseminate stresses spreading information to many recipients and is formal.

items.pt: comunicar à polícia a ocorrência de
items.example: The caretaker notified the police of the break-in.
items.note: The pattern is notify someone of something, often in official contexts.

items.example: Despite the accusations, the driver continued to protest his innocence.
items.note: Here protest means firmly declare innocence, not organise a demonstration.

items.example: The director professed ignorance of the missing records.
items.note: Often suggests a claim of not knowing that may be doubtful or insincere.

items.pt: dar a notícia a alguém, geralmente ruim
items.example: She asked her brother to help break the news to their parents.
items.note: Used especially for telling someone news likely to be upsetting.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: His repeated protestations of innocence did not persuade the jury.
items.note: Protestation refers to a declaration; protest alone usually suggests opposition.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: The project begins with a short statement of aims.
items.note: A formal noun phrase common in reports and organisational documents.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: Rapid dissemination of information helped residents prepare.
items.note: The nominal form of disseminate information stresses widespread distribution.

items.pt: comunicação de um crime às autoridades
items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: The organisation has a clear procedure for notification of a crime.
items.note: Notification is the formal noun for informing an authority.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: The declaration of the winner was delayed by an appeal.
items.note: The noun declaration names a formal announcement.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: The territory voted to declare independence after years of debate.
items.note: Declare combines with independence for a formal political statement.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: Several community groups declared support for the new library.
items.note: Formal, public statement of backing for a person or cause.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: The leader threatened to declare war on the neighbouring state.
items.note: May be literal or figurative; on is the normal preposition.

items.section: Exercises · Derived forms and usage contrasts
items.example: A grant proposal should state goals clearly before discussing costs.
items.note: Goals commonly collocates with state; clearly describes explicit expression.

units.title: Unit 10 — Collocations with phrasal verbs
learningObjectives: Match phrasal verbs with their natural partners in news reports and formal decisions.
Use everyday phrasal verb collocations with time, plans, expectations and language practice.
Choose the correct particles and fixed complements in high-frequency phrasal verb expressions.
Distinguish formal adherence to principles from idiomatic expressions for defeating opponents or using savings.

items.section: A · News reports and formal decisions
items.example: All parties agreed to abide by the panel’s decision.
items.note: Formal: accept and comply with a decision; by is essential.

items.section: A · News reports and formal decisions
items.example: The newly elected mayor will take up office in January.
items.note: Formal phrase meaning begin an official role, not physically occupy a room.

items.pt: agir com base em uma denúncia ou informação sigilosa
items.section: A · News reports and formal decisions
items.example: Detectives acted on a tip-off and found the stolen instruments.
items.note: A tip-off is confidential information prompting action, often by the police.

items.section: A · News reports and formal decisions
items.example: The design team came up with an alternative to the original layout.
items.note: Come up with means devise or suggest an idea; with must stay in the phrase.

items.section: A · News reports and formal decisions
items.example: After months apart, the couple decided to file for divorce.
items.note: Legal wording for formally applying for divorce; use for, not to.

items.section: A · News reports and formal decisions
items.example: The regulator plans to come down heavily on repeat offenders.
items.note: Means impose strong sanctions; often follows a policy or enforcement decision.

items.pt: absorver o clima ou a atmosfera do lugar
items.example: We arrived early to soak up the atmosphere before the concert.
items.note: Figuratively means enjoy and absorb the mood of a place or event.

items.example: Could you free up some time for a planning call tomorrow?
items.note: Free up means make something available by changing existing commitments.

items.example: I listen to Spanish radio to keep up my Spanish.
items.note: Keep up with language skills means practise enough to maintain them.

items.example: Reading every morning helps you keep up your English.
items.note: A natural language-learning application of keep up.

items.example: A long walk through the park helped us work up an appetite.
items.note: Means become hungry through activity; work in an appetite is incorrect.

items.example: A brief visit would fit in with our weekend plans.
items.note: Fit in with expresses compatibility with an existing schedule.

items.example: The upgraded software did not live up to our expectations.
items.note: The established preposition sequence is up to, not on to.

items.example: The students burst into laughter at the unexpected joke.
items.note: Burst into marks a sudden start, with laughter as a fixed noun partner.

items.example: She burst into tears when she heard the farewell speech.
items.note: Means suddenly start crying; tears is a common partner of burst into.

items.example: We had to dip into savings to replace the broken heater.
items.note: Spend part of money previously set aside, often reluctantly.

items.example: The association may dip into emergency funds to fix the roof.
items.note: Dip into stresses using only some of a reserved amount.

items.example: Please jot down an address before your phone battery dies.
items.note: Jot down means write a short piece of information quickly.

items.example: I had to jot down a phone number on a receipt.
items.note: Phone number is a typical information object for jot down.

items.pt: anotar rapidamente um número de sala
items.example: The visitor jotted down a room number at reception.
items.note: Jot down is especially natural with brief details worth remembering.

items.example: The security guards managed to see off an intruder.
items.note: See off can mean successfully repel or drive away an unwanted person.

items.example: The home team saw off a tough opponent in the final.
items.note: In competition, see off means defeat, not merely say goodbye.

items.example: She refused the offer because she wanted to adhere to her principles.
items.note: Formal combination meaning consistently follow principles or standards.

items.example: The community continued to adhere to its beliefs despite criticism.
items.note: To is required after adhere when discussing convictions.

items.example: Campaigners urged the organisation to adhere to its ideals.
items.note: Adhere to is more formal than stick to in this context.

items.example: The school continues to adhere to a philosophy of inclusive learning.
items.note: A philosophy is a natural abstract object of adhere to.

items.example: Engineers came up with a solution that reduced energy use.
items.note: Extends the taught come up with an alternative pattern to an idiomatic proposal.

items.example: The company must live up to its promise of faster support.
items.note: The same pattern used with expectations also takes promises.

items.example: Automation could free up resources for essential maintenance.
items.note: An idiomatic extension of freeing up time by making capacity available.
